questions.q: In classical decomposition, what is the remainder?
options: The part of the series that trend and season do not explain
why: Correct. In the additive case it is y − trend − season.
The mean is a single number, not a series.
That is a seasonal difference, a different operation.

questions.q: Monthly data. What window length does the classical trend use, and how many values does it lose in total at the two ends?
questions.why: The period is 12, so m / 2 = 6 values are lost at each end: 6 + 6 = 12 values in total.

questions.q: Period 4, values 8, 12, 16, 10, 10. Compute the 2×4 trend at the third value.
Raw additive seasonal averages for 3 positions are 2, 5, 11. What is the centered index of the third position?
Airline passengers: the seasonal peak grows as the number of passengers grows. Which decomposition?
why: Correct. The peak is a percentage of the level.
The additive form would force a constant swing.

questions.q: You decompose a series with a centered moving average, then use the 'trend' column as an input feature of a forecast model, for the same day. What is the problem?
options: The trend at day t uses values from after day t (leakage)
The model cannot use a trend
why: Correct. A centered average looks into the future. The model sees information it will not have when it forecasts.
It is NaN only at the ends.
Models can use trend features if they are computed without the future.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of STL over classical decomposition?
options: The seasonal part can change over time and the trend covers the ends
It works only for multiplicative data
why: Correct. It also has a robust option for outliers.
STL is additive. Use a log for multiplicative data.
